title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

hero.subtitle: A major overhaul of TLS that eliminates legacy cruft, reduces handshake latency to one round trip, and mandates forward secrecy.

steps.label: ClientHello + KeyShare
steps.description: Cipher suites + key material in one shot

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 is a major revision of the TLS protocol that provides significant improvements in both security and performance. It removes obsolete and unsafe features and streamlines the handshake.

TLS 1.2
TLS 1.3
2-RTT handshake
1-RTT handshake (0-RTT resumption)
RSA key exchange
(EC)DHE only - forward secrecy mandatory
CBC & RC4 ciphers
AEAD only (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305)
Compression supported
Compression removed (CRIME attack)
Renegotiation
Removed entirely
sections.eli5: TLS 1.3 is the newer, tidier version of the way computers keep their conversations secret. It is faster and safer than the old version.

sections.title: 1-RTT Handshake
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 reduces the handshake to a single round trip by having the client send key shares in the first message.

ClientHello
Client sends supported cipher suites, key shares for likely groups, and random. Everything needed for key exchange in one message.
ServerHello
Server responds with its key share. From this point, all further messages are encrypted.
EncryptedExtensions
Server extensions that don't need to be in the clear are now encrypted.
sections.eli5: The client sends its secret-sharing ingredients up front, so the two sides can agree on a secret after just one back-and-forth. Then they hide the rest of the setup chat too.

sections.title: 0-RTT Resumption
sections.content:
When a client has previously connected to a server, it can send application data in its first message (0-RTT) using a pre-shared key from the previous session.

0-RTT data is not protected against replay attacks. Servers must ensure that 0-RTT data is idempotent or implement replay protection at the application layer.
sections.eli5: If you have visited before, you can start talking in your very first message. The catch is that someone could copy that first message and send it again, so it should only carry things that are safe to repeat.

sections.title: Removed Features
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 aggressively removed legacy features that were sources of security vulnerabilities:

Static RSANo forward secrecy; removed in favor of ephemeral key exchange
CBC CiphersVulnerable to padding oracle attacks (POODLE, Lucky13)
RC4Statistical biases allow plaintext recovery
CompressionEnables the CRIME side-channel attack
RenegotiationComplex, attack-prone mechanism removed entirely
Custom DHE GroupsOnly named groups with known security properties allowed
sections.eli5: The designers threw out the old tools that had been broken or tricked by attackers, so nobody can choose them by mistake.

sections.title: Cipher Suites
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 dramatically simplifies cipher suite negotiation. Only five cipher suites are defined:

TLS 1.3 Cipher Suites
TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256
TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256
TLS_AES_128_CCM_SHA256
TLS_AES_128_CCM_8_SHA256

Key exchange and authentication algorithms are negotiated separately via extensions, not as part of the cipher suite. This greatly simplifies the combinatorial explosion of TLS 1.2.
sections.eli5: There is now a very short menu of ways to scramble messages. Picking the lock type and the key swap are done separately.

references.text: Rescorla, E., "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3", RFC 8446, August 2018.
Dierks, T. and E. Rescorla, "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.2", RFC 5246, August 2008.

subtitle: A major overhaul of TLS that removes legacy features, needs one round trip to set up, and requires forward secrecy.
summary: TLS 1.3 is the current version of the protocol that encrypts most traffic on the web. It cuts the handshake to one round trip, encrypts more of the handshake itself, and drops older algorithms and features that proved unsafe. A resumed connection can send data in its first flight (0-RTT), with weaker replay protection.

eli5.summary: Two computers need to agree on a secret code before they talk. TLS 1.3 lets them agree on it in a single back-and-forth and throws out all the old, leaky ways of doing it.

tldr.problem: TLS 1.2 had slow handshakes and kept many old, attackable options.
tldr.mechanism: The client guesses a key-exchange group and sends its key share in the ClientHello, so the server can reply with its share and encrypt everything after the ServerHello.
tldr.outcome: A one-round-trip handshake with forward secrecy by default, authenticated encryption only, and far fewer options to misconfigure.

questions: what is the difference between tls 1.2 and tls 1.3
how many round trips does the tls 1.3 handshake take
which cipher suites does tls 1.3 support
why was rsa key exchange removed from tls
today: TLS 1.3 is supported by all major browsers, servers and TLS libraries, and a large share of HTTPS traffic uses it. HTTP/3 over QUIC builds its handshake on TLS 1.3. Operators commonly keep TLS 1.2 enabled for older clients, but disable earlier versions. RFC 9846 later obsoleted RFC 8446 with a revised specification of TLS 1.3.

implementations.note: Widely deployed TLS 1.3 stacks in browsers and servers.

messages.label: ClientHello + key_share
messages.note: Offers cipher suites and (EC)DHE key shares for the groups it guesses the server supports.

messages.label: ServerHello + key_share
messages.note: Selects the parameters and returns its key share. Everything after this is encrypted.

messages.label: EncryptedExtensions
messages.note: Extensions that do not need to be in the clear.

messages.label: Finished
messages.note: Client confirms the handshake. Application data can now flow both ways.
